source.title: Know Your Limits: Entropy Estimation Modeling for Compression and Generalization

record.tranche_reason: The study measures language-model cross-entropy at different training-token counts, but uses newly introduced encoder-augmented models and does not reproduce the original power-law fitting procedure.
record.gate_note: The study reports token-scaled losses in Table 1 and qualitative scaling comparisons in Section 5.1. It does not fit or report power-law exponents. Other architectural and quantization results are not included because they do not report the scaling claim's loss-versus-parameters, tokens, or compute relation.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces encoder-augmented 'entropy estimation models' and compares their training efficiency with causal transformers. Its only loss-vs-scale numbers are two token counts (13.1 and 32.8 BT, about 2.5x) in Table 1, with no power-law fit, no parameter or compute sweep, and no test of any scaling-law form. It cites Hoffmann et al. only as background. It neither tests nor relies on the scaling claim, so it does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is incomplete. The authors conclude that encoder-augmented entropy estimation models train more efficiently and compress better than compute-matched causal transformers, with better sample scaling. They also show how per-token entropy estimates can be obtained, including via second-order models. They prove that training below dataset entropy harms generalization, and show empirically that entropy-informed loss rescaling improves causal-model generalization (best eval loss 3.280 vs 3.515). They note that whether the gains hold at very large compute is untested.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces encoder-augmented causal decoder architectures and compares their loss scaling with causal models; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Evaluation context changes the reported loss: full-context losses are higher than All Samples losses, with the authors describing the difference as nearly constant across the two training scales. The paper also reports scaling comparisons for transformer and masked-mixer architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Authors report that the loss gap between EEMs and causal models, relative to causal-model loss, grows exponentially with training samples (Fig. 4, Fig. S5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Encoder-augmented entropy estimation models have better sample scaling than compute-matched causal transformers, and the gap widens with tokens.

record.problems: The loss-scaling evidence covers only two reported training-token counts in Table 1, and no power-law fit or uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors state that limited compute prevented direct tests of some scaling hypotheses at very large scales.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling results left out.

untested.parts: No power-law fit; only two token counts for causal LMs; no parameter or compute scaling of absolute loss.
No extrapolation of small-run fits to larger runs. The paper's 46B/300B-token forecasts for its own EEM are not scaling-law tests.
Head and kernel variations are reported only as training-efficiency curves for autoencoders and EEMs, not as a fixed-parameter shape test of LM loss.

record.verdict_notes: I override the reader's 'tests/T2' and V1 limits_scope label. The scaling content is an architectural efficiency comparison over 75-250M-parameter models and 13-33B tokens, with two reported token points. It bears on no version of the scaling-law claim. EEM rows are unlinked because the model is non-causal.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports loss at 13.1 and 32.8 billion training tokens, but does not fit a power law, test scaling over several orders of magnitude, or measure loss scaling in parameters or compute.
No power laws fitted on small runs are evaluated against runs orders of magnitude larger. The paper gives a forecast for its own model, but does not test that form of extrapolation.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimising allocation between parameters and tokens is tested.
Architecture variants are explored, but the study does not test whether depth, width, or other details change loss only slightly at a fixed parameter count.
The paper mentions possible use in other modalities but reports no scaling results for other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task performance is measured as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare scaling-law fitting choices or exponents, or test whether curves depart from a single power law.
